name: Contracts, warranties, and change management in painting projects
headline: Contracts, warranties, and change management in painting projects
articleBody: Consumer protection agencies and construction-industry organizations emphasize clear written agreements for interior painting to reduce disputes. The Federal Trade Commission’s home improvement guidance advises homeowners to insist on a detailed contract that describes the scope of work, materials (including specific paint brands, product lines, and sheen levels), preparation standards, start and completion dates, and payment schedule. State and local consumer affairs departments in California reinforce these points and add that contracts should identify license numbers for licensed contractors, include required notices, and clearly state how change orders will be handled. Trade association guidance for painting contractors recommends specifying the number of coats, primer requirements, and whether colors will change. These documents also suggest defining exclusions, such as lead abatement, wallpaper removal, or repair of hidden substrate damage, which may require separate pricing once discovered. Warranties are typically limited to defects in workmanship for a defined period, often one to three years in residential work, and do not usually cover normal wear, abuse, or issues caused by moisture or structural movement. Manufacturer warranties on paint products are separate and focus on the performance of the coating under proper application conditions. Change orders are a common source of misunderstanding. Industry best practices and construction law primers advise that any change to the agreed scope—such as additional rooms, upgraded paint lines, or unexpected repairs—should be documented in writing with corresponding cost and schedule impacts before the extra work is performed. This applies equally to residential and commercial interior projects. Consumer advisories in California also warn against large upfront payments and encourage using milestone or progress payments aligned with completed work, helping ensure that the financial terms match the realities of the interior painting process.
